notes.meaning: Everything that exists had a beginning, and God made it. "Created" here means God made the world out of nothing, with no material already there. "In the beginning" is the start of time itself, and "the heavens and the earth" means the whole universe. Many older teachers also see a quiet hint of the Trinity in the plural Hebrew name for God. The Trinity means one God in three Persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

At first the earth was shapeless and empty. It was a dark mass covered by water, with nothing living in it yet. God's Spirit was hovering over it like a mother bird brooding over her young, ready to bring order and life. Matthew Henry sees here a picture of a heart without God: dark, empty, and confused until God's grace makes it new.

differ.view: Some believe the earth may have lain broken and dark for long ages between verse 1 and verse 2, before God began the six days.

notes.meaning: God simply spoke, and light appeared at once. His word is all the power that is needed. Light came before the sun was made, which shows that God does not depend on the sun to give light. Teachers also compare this to the way God first shines His light into a sinner's heart (2 Corinthians 4:6).

God looked at the light and found it good, exactly as He meant it to be. He does not need to inspect His work, but this teaches us to agree with His verdict on what He makes. He also set light and darkness apart so that they take turns as day and night.

God named the light "day" and the darkness "night." Naming them shows He is Lord over both. Evening comes before morning because the Hebrew day began at sunset. The older commentators take this as a real, ordinary day. Calvin adds that God spread His work over six days so we would slow down and think about it.

differ.view: Some have tried to fit the creation days to the long ages taught by geology.

notes.meaning: On the second day God made an "expanse," something spread out like a curtain: the sky. It divides the waters below, like the seas, from the waters above, which are the clouds that give rain. Moses describes the world as ordinary people see it, not like an astronomy book. God named the expanse "sky." This is the only day without the words "it was good," perhaps because the work with the waters was not finished until the next day.

God gathered the waters into seas so that dry land could appear. He named the land "earth" and the waters "seas." God still sets the borders of the sea so that it does not cover the land (Job 38:8-11). Matthew Henry says God was now building a home for people to live in.

At God's word the bare ground became green with grass, plants, and fruit trees. Each one carried its own seed and reproduced after its kind, so plant life would keep going for every generation. The plants appeared full-grown and fruitful, all in a day. They came before the sun to show that growth comes from God, not from the sun. This closed the third day.

God made lights in the sky. They separate day from night and mark seasons, days, and years, which helps farmers and gives order to life. They also give light to the earth. The "signs" are things like weather and times, not fortune-telling, and Scripture warns against fearing signs in the sky (Jeremiah 10:2). These lights shine for our good.

God made two great lights: the sun for the day and the moon for the night. He made the stars too. Moses speaks of them as they look to us. The moon is "great" because of how much light it gives the earth, not because of its size. They "rule" only as God's servants, by giving light.

God Himself put these lights in their places to shine on the earth and keep day and night apart. This shows how foolish it is to worship the sun, moon, or stars. They are creatures made to serve us, not gods. God saw that it was good.

This closed the fourth day. Matthew Henry says the daily turning of day and night calls us to pray and praise God every morning and evening. Adam Clarke and John Gill also note a picture here: the sun appeared on the fourth day, and Christ, the "Sun of righteousness," came about four thousand years after creation.

On the fifth day God filled the waters with swarms of living things and the sky with birds. These are the first living creatures in the story. Creation keeps moving up, step by step, from simpler things to greater ones.

God created the great sea creatures, such as whales and other huge sea animals, along with every swimming thing and every bird, each after its kind. His wisdom shows in the tiny as much as in the huge, in an ant as much as in an elephant. God saw that it was good.

God blessed the fish and birds and told them to multiply. His blessing actually gave them the power to have young. Every new generation of fish and birds still comes from that blessing. This closed the fifth day.

On the sixth day God made the land animals in three groups: livestock that can be tamed, small creeping things, and wild animals. The ground had no power of its own to make them. God made each one after its kind, with its own nature and way of life. God saw that it was good.

Now God's tone changes from a command to a plan: "Let Us make man." This shows that people are special. The older Christian teachers see the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit agreeing together here, not God talking to angels. "Image" and "likeness" mean the same thing. That image lies mainly in the soul: a mind that knows God, a will that obeys Him, and true holiness. People were also given the job of ruling over the animals.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars read "Us" as God speaking in a royal "we," or as God speaking to the angels of His court.

notes.meaning: God did what He had planned and made people in His image, both male and female. Jesus pointed back to this one man and one woman when He taught about marriage (Matthew 19:4-5). Because every person comes from that first couple, we are one family. Sin has since damaged God's image in us, but God renews it by His grace.

God blessed the first couple and told them to have children, fill the earth, and take care of it and rule over it. Children are a gift of His blessing, given within marriage. People were to manage the earth under God and give Him the praise. The fall into sin weakened this rule, but did not end it.

God gave people seed plants and fruit for food, and gave the animals green plants. Many older teachers think people did not eat meat until after the Flood (Genesis 9:3), though Calvin was not sure. Either way, God provided richly before anyone asked. Matthew Henry says that He who feeds the birds will not let His children go hungry.

God looked at everything and called it "very good." Every part was just as He meant, with no flaw, and the whole fit together beautifully, crowned by the making of people. God could have made it all in an instant. He chose six days to show His wisdom step by step and to set a pattern of six days of work and a day of rest.
